item.title: Roads, Trails, and Rails West
item.snippet: White settlers moved west first by trail and then by train. Explore the opening of the Western United States with this map.
item.description:
Note: Explore this map with the activity Rails and Trails West.

In the beginning of the 1800s, many Americans thought of the West as a wild, uninhabited place. Rugged frontiersmen and explorers shared tales of endless natural resources. The population of the United States was growing. The industrial economy was also growing, but many people still made their living as farmers. Poor farming practices caused soils to become less fertile, and farmland was becoming crowded. As a result, Americans began to push farther west looking for new land.  

The term Manifest Destiny was created in 1845. In popular culture, white journalists, musicians, and politicians imagined the West as an empty land of plenty. Manifest Destiny suggested that people of European descent had a responsibility to take over the land. The phrase created an ideal picture of westward migration. But people who believed in Manifest Destiny ignored the fact that the land was not truly empty. Indigenous and Hispanic people already lived in many areas.  

The trails and railways they built crossed the lands of many Native nations, and conflict sometimes happened between indigenous people and settlers. In many cases, despite multiple treaties and promises, the U.S. government and primarily white settlers didn't recognize or respect indigenous land claims. Indigenous people who tried to defend their land from white settlement were seen by the U.S. government as the aggressors. As a result of westward expansion, many Native nations lost all or most of their land.

item.title: Indigenous Territories
item.snippet: Explore a map layer of Indigenous territories worldwide, provided by the Native Lands Digital API (2025).
item.description:
This map layer was created by Native Land Digital, a Canadian nonprofit organization that strives to map Indigenous lands. Many Indigenous peoples do not view land, or land ownership, in the same way that non-Indigenous peoples do. As a result, this map does not look like a parcel map you would find at your local auditor’s office with clear boundaries that meet along a clear border. Additionally, this map accounts for many different time periods and lists groups together that may not have been contemporaries. This map updates weekly as new territories are added and existing ones are updated as new information is discovered.

 

This map attempts to show a picture of the historic territories of the people who lived there before the period of colonization, a time that for many Indigenous people brought hardships, suffering, and genocide. Explore the area where you live now. Who else has lived there?

Disclaimer from Native Lands Digital: This map does not represent or intend to represent official or legal boundaries of any Indigenous nations. To learn about definitive boundaries, contact the nations in question.

Also, this map is not perfect - it is a work in progress with tons of contributions from the community. Please send your fixes to Native Land Digital if you find errors.

You are free to use this data layer for your own maps and applications, but we encourage you to add a similar disclaimer on your own resource.

Data citation: Native Lands Digital (2026) Native Land Maps https://native-land.ca/maps/native-land.

You can also explore this dataset in the ArcGIS Living Atlas.

item.title: Railroads 1826 to 1911
item.snippet: Provide as accurate as possible location of historical railroads in the United States from earliest times (1826-7) at intervals throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth century (currently ending in 1911)
item.description:
In the 1800s, the spread of railroads enabled the growth and spread of the United States. Although slow by today’s standards, trains traveled more quickly than other forms of transportation available at the time. By train, it took roughly four days to reach San Francisco from Omaha, Nebraska. By contrast, it had taken covered wagons four to six months, and stagecoaches around a month. 


 

In addition to travel, railroads facilitated trade and economic growth. Prior to railroads, people relied on a system of roads and canals for transportation of goods and crops. But this system could be unreliable depending on road conditions, the weather, and many other factors. Trains brought products made in the factories of the East and Midwest to the rest of the country and carried farm produce and livestock to urban markets. 


 

The first railroad charter was granted to John Stevens in 1815, and several railroads were in service by 1830. Early rail development was haphazard, financed by individual investors and built without government oversight. Rail gauges, or the distance between rails, could be different depending on the company. This caused a lot of problems for connecting railroads, because only trains designed for that gauge could use those sections of track. Despite miles of track being built, people were generally still skeptical about the usefulness of railroads. In 1843, the Western Railroad of Massachusetts proved to Americans that trains could transport crops and other goods long distances at low costs.  


 

By 1861, there were 35,400 kilometers (22,000 miles) of track in the North and only 15,300 kilometers (9,500 miles) in the South. Troops and supplies could be transported quickly using trains. Many battles, like the Battle of Bull Run, were fought over control of Southern railway depots, and tracks were used to move both Confederate and Union soldiers to battles.  


 

After the Civil War, railway construction increased significantly. In 1862, Congress passed the Pacific Railway Act with the goal of building a transcontinental railroad. The first, built by the Central Pacific Railroad Company in the West and the Union Pacific in the Midwest, was completed in 1869. Following roughly the route previously taken by the Pony Express and the California Trail, the route was called the Overland Route.  


 

Construction was dangerous, as rail crews had to cross mountains, rivers, and other difficult terrain. For this work, the Central Pacific and Union Pacific relied mainly on immigrant labor, recruiting Chinese immigrants in the West and Irish immigrants in the Midwest. Formerly enslaved people and Mormons were also part of these crews. Between 10,000 and 15,000 Chinese workers completed an estimated 90 percent of work on the Central Pacific’s portion of track, facing racism, violence, and discrimination. Chinese workers were often paid less than white workers and were given the most undesirable and dangerous jobs. 


 

The Overland Route was one of the first land-grant railroads. To fund construction of such a long and expensive project, the U.S. government gave railroad companies millions of acres of land that they could sell for profit. Following this model, many more railroads were built, including four additional transcontinental railroads. These new railroads took southern and northern routes across the country. 


 

In addition to connecting existing cities on the West Coast to the rest of the country, the railroads also influenced where people settled. Trains made multiple stops to refuel, make repairs, and take on more food and water. In return, towns grew around these stops. More than 7,000 cities and towns west of the Missouri River started as Union Pacific depots and water stops. 


 

In 1890, the U.S. Bureau of the Census announced that the “Frontier was closed.” The railroads had played a large role in that milestone. 


 

This dataset was researched and built by Dr. Jeremy Atack, Professor Emeritus and Research Professor of Economics at Vanderbilt University. His procedure and sources, as well as downloadable files, are documented here.

item.title: Trails West
item.snippet: This U.S. National Park Service layer (2023) illustrates trails used for Westward emigration and trade in the 1800s.
item.description:
This layer shows seven trails that link the Western United States with the Midwest. These routes are the Oregon Trail, California Trail, Mormon Pioneer Trail, Old Spanish Trail, Santa Fe Trail, Butterfield Overland Express Trail, and Pony Express Trail. Between the 1830s and 1860s, these trails were used heavily by emigrants looking for new economic opportunities in the west. The Oregon and California Trails, for example, were used by hundreds of thousands of emigrants looking for new farmland or opportunities in mining. As more settlers moved west, the trails were also used to transport mail and goods and to to link settlers to the Eastern states. 


 

Travel over these trails was often difficult and dangerous. Routes took travelers through prairies, deserts, and mountain ranges. Emigrants primarily used prairie schooners, or small covered wagons, to carry their belongings. Covered wagons were often pulled by oxen, and traveled an average of 24 to 32 kilometers (15-20 miles) per day. Stagecoaches were also used to transport travelers, mail, and packages. Some mail carriers, like the famous Pony Express, made the trip on horseback.
 


 

Westward expansion during this time is often described by the term "manifest destiny." White journalists invented the term in 1845 to describe what they considered a divine responsibility to settle the Western United States. But this idea ignored the fact that many indigenous and Hispanic people already lived in the West. 
 


 
These trails cross the lands of many Native nations, and conflict sometimes happened between indigenous people and settlers. In many cases, despite multiple treaties and promises, the U.S. government and primarily white settlers didn't recognize indigenous land claims. Indigenous people who tried to defend their land from white settlement were seen by the U.S. government as the aggressors. As a result of westward expansion, many Native nations lost all or most of their land.


 

Today, these routes are Congressionally designated National Historic Trails, and are maintained by U.S. federal and state agencies including the National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management, and others.
